newsitem.title: USA: Argentina, Brazil debts firmer on credit upgrade.
newsitem.headline: Argentina, Brazil debts firmer on credit upgrade.

text.p: Argentina and Brazil grabbed the limelight in emerging market debt trading after their long-term foreign currency debts were upgraded a notch, but market appetite for those issues turned out to be less than robust, traders said.
Standard & Poor's, a U.S. credit rating agency, raised the long-term currency debt of Argentina to double B from double B minus and of Brazil to double B minus from single B plus.

The news was a tonic to the Latin debts after a week of heavy selling in response to higher U.S. interest rates, but spreads were unchanged to about 5 basis points tighter mainly on short-covering, traders said.
The enthusiasm was kept in check by the general wariness over U.S. interest rates, they said.
"It's good news for the market," said Marcelo Fleury, a vice president at Garban Corp, who noted that, except for some short-covering, investors by and large remained on the sidelines.
The most liquid Brazil C, which had traded an intraday high of 75-3/16 and slid to 74-7/16 before the rating announcement, merely recovered to 75.00 bid, up 1/4 on the day.
Argetnina debt papers did not fare much better, with the bellwether Argentina FRB adding a tiny 1/8 to 89-3/4 bid.
"There's a lot of hesitancy," said a Brady trader. "People are looking at the long bond and the stock market."
Some also considered that Argentina's debts had already priced in the upgrade, since last month an S&P executive said in Buenos Aires that Argentina was under review for upgrade, he said.
For Brazil, the upgrade, which was not as widely anticipated, failed to dispel the unease that many investors felt about Brazil's mounting trade deficit, the trader said.
Brazil posted a $1.026 billion trade deficit in March, bringing the country's first quarter trade gap to about $3.06 billion.
Garban's Fleury noted that the upgrade would give Brazil impetus to raise capital in the global markets before rising U.S. rates further cloud the outlook.

Among the East European and Russian debt papers, Bulgaria continued its recovery. Caretaker Finance Minister Svetoslav Gavriiski said the country is already functining under the conditions of a currency board.
Russia enjoyed a small rally in European trading as Michel Camdessus, director general of the International Monetary Fund, said it was time to resume lending to Russia.
But U.S. traders remained cautious, pointing out that the January and February tranches of the three-year $10 billion loan were still withheld.
In addition, they said a major investment bank predicted that the closing of the Vnesh loan restructuring would be delayed from mid-1997 to September.
Russia Vnesh was unchanged at 78.00 bid.
